newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists would set euro policy - Jospin.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists would set euro policy - Jospin.

text.p: French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said on Wednesday his party would impose its line on a single European currency on its Communist allies if the left won a parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1.

In a France-Inter radio interview, Jospin was asked how he would reconcile differences between the Socialists, who favour European economic and monetary union with conditions, and the Communists, who oppose it and want a new referendum.

He said the Communists had evolved positively on Europe, but added: "In any case I told (Communist leader) Robert Hue that if there is a majority in which the Socialists have a far bigger contingent to the Communist party...there can only be one line: the one set by the French people which gave the parliamentary majority to the candidates of this party."
The ruling centre-right government has warned voters that France could isolate itself within the European Union if they elect a left-wing coalition with two contradictory positions on monetary union.
But Jospin said: "There won't be both a 'yes' and a 'no' to the single currency. There will be a single line, the one which (we) propose to the French people.

"Then it will be up to the Communists to make up their minds freely if we have a majority. They will only be able to participate in government if they are ready to commit themselves to that line," he insisted.

He added that it would be better if the Communists committed themselves for the duration of the five-year legislature rather than dropping out of government in mid-term as they did in the 1984 under Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.

The Socialists' conditions for a single currency are the creation of a European "economic government" as a counterweight to the independent central bank, the inclusion of Italy and Spain in the first wave of members, no overvaluation of the euro against the dollar and a pact for growth and solidarity to promote jobs.

The opposition has also said it would reject any further austerity measures to meet the Maastricht criterion of limiting public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product to qualify for a single currency in 1999.
Jospin said the Communists and Socialists were at least honest in not hiding their differences.
There were deep differences on Europe in the ruling coalition, notably between Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Eurosceptics Charles Pasqua and Philippe Seguin, he charged.
